The money · ceilings, each one shown, never summed

The largest ceilings

In the twelve months to Sep 22, 2026, 68 county-side resolutions carried a “not to exceed” ceiling; 2 more are a ceiling the chamber later rescinded, or the rescission itself, and are left out. Of those, 21 are new authorizations the chamber voted through and 35 restate a contract’s total (a change order or an amendment); 12 sit on the September 22, 2026 agenda with votes not read yet. The largest new authorization the chamber voted through was $606,998 (IF-160-25); the largest restated contract total, $2,994,000 (IF-179-25), sits in its own group below. Ceilings are permission, not payments, and are deliberately never summed into one headline: change orders restate a whole contract’s total as the work changes, refunding bonds reissue existing debt, and the biggest figures on record are IDA bond issues the county approves but never spends. The county ledger shows what was actually spent.

How this register is built

The record, verified against itself

Sources. The Niagara County Legislature publishes agendas, resolution packets, and meeting minutes for every session at niagaracounty.gov. This register parses the 2015–2026 era — the years where full resolution texts and minutes are posted. Meetings from 2007–2014 are on the county site as agenda lists only, so they are deliberately excluded rather than shown half-built.

The tie-out. Each meeting’s agenda prints its own list of resolution numbers. Every parsed resolution is checked against that list; the parse of a meeting fails loudly rather than publishing a partial read.

✓ 6,051 resolutions parsed across 182 meetings (the count includes 6 meetings with no readable resolutions) · every id tied out against its meeting’s own agenda list · 97% of votes matched where minutes are machine-readable

What a machine cannot read. 532 of the 6,051 resolutions sit in meetings whose posted minutes are photocopier scans with no text layer. For those, this register reads the page images with the OCR engine built into Windows — locally, from the county’s own PDFs — and recovered 500 votes. Every OCR-read vote is labeled as such on its record; a tally is refused unless it fits the chamber’s 15 seats, and no dollar figure is ever taken from OCR text — where OCR is the only source, the money stays blank rather than guessed. Beyond that, 5 resolutions sit in scans OCR could not read, 42 in meetings whose minutes the county never posted and 98 in the meeting of September 22, 2026, held but with minutes not posted yet. Against minutes with a native text layer, 5,187 of 5,374 votes are matched (97%). 21 documents the county’s site no longer serves were recovered from the Internet Archive’s crawl of niagaracounty.gov; their source links point to the archived copies. Where the record is still unreadable, this register says so and links the image. The full per-meeting ledger is published at data/coverage.json.

Honesty notes. The county’s PDFs carry a machine text layer with light OCR noise (“CmTied” for “Carried”, the digit 1 read as the letter I); parsing tolerates the known artifacts and otherwise reports what is printed, including vote totals that occasionally disagree with the chamber’s seat count. Where the printed counts and the recorded outcome disagree, the row says “record says …” rather than choose. Dollar figures are read from the resolution text: “up to” amounts are authorization ceilings, other figures are amounts mentioned in the text (bid tabulations include losing bids) — neither is a payment record. A figure mentioned in the text is never ranked, and one larger than the county’s entire year of spending (its own filing with the State Comptroller) is flagged unverified. Votes shown as unmatched simply were not found by the parser in that meeting’s minutes; the minutes remain the authority.
